title: Longest Climb on a Grid
statement:
You get a grid of integers grid. A climb starts at any cell and repeatedly steps to a neighbouring cell (up, down, left or right, never diagonally, never off the grid) whose value is strictly greater than the current one.

Return the number of cells in the longest possible climb. A single cell on its own is a climb of length 1.

examples.why: 1 → 2 → 3 → … → 9 spirals through every cell. Climbs may turn and go up or left, not only right and down.
Each step must go strictly higher, so equal neighbours cannot be chained.
1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 6 → 7. Starting at the smallest value 0 gives only 2, because 0 is boxed in by 9, 8 and 7.

hints: Fix a starting cell. The longest climb from it is 1 plus the longest climb from its best higher neighbour. Does that answer depend on how you reached the cell?
It does not, and a climb can never loop back because values strictly increase. So best[r][c], the longest climb starting at (r, c), can be computed once and reused. No visited set is needed.

Memoized DFS: best[r][c] = 1 + max(best of strictly higher neighbours), or 1 if none. Or avoid recursion: process cells from the highest value to the lowest, so every higher neighbour is already finished when you reach a cell.

explain.intuition:
Here the table is the grid itself. Let best[r][c] be the length of the longest climb that starts at cell (r, c). Read it off the first decision: which neighbour do you step to? Only strictly higher neighbours are allowed, and after the step you face the same question from there. So best[r][c] = 1 + max(best[n]) over higher neighbours n, or 1 at a local peak. The answer is the largest best anywhere.

Two facts make this safe. The value of best[r][c] does not depend on how you got to (r, c), so it can be cached. And the "higher neighbour" arrows can never form a cycle, because values strictly rise along them: the arrows form a DAG, like an import graph without circular imports. That is why the DFS needs no visited set and why the memo never sees a half-finished cell. Since it is a DAG, any topological order also works: sort the cells by value, highest first, and fill best in that order with no recursion at all. Each cell's higher neighbours are done by the time it is reached.
steps: Make best, a grid of zeros meaning "not computed yet".
dfs(r, c): if best[r][c] is set, return it. Otherwise start at 1, and for each in-bounds neighbour with a strictly greater value take max(·, 1 + dfs(neighbour)). Store and return it.
Call dfs on every cell and return the largest result.
Without recursion: list all cells, sort them by value from high to low, and apply the same rule in that order. Equal neighbours are never used, so their relative order does not matter.
pitfalls: Allowing equal neighbours (≥ instead of >). Then the arrows can form cycles, the memo returns half-built values, and the second example would not be 1.
Only starting from the smallest value or from local minima of the whole grid. The third example's 0 is a dead end.

Recursing without a memo. A plain DFS from every cell redoes the same climbs and blows up exponentially on grids with many branching paths. Deep recursion is the other risk: a snake-shaped grid makes one climb as long as the whole grid, which is why the grid here is capped and why the sorted order is worth knowing.

complexity.time: O(R · C) with the memo; O(R · C · log(R · C)) with the sort

solutions.title: Plain DFS from every cell
solutions.idea: From each cell, try every strictly higher neighbour recursively. Correct, but the same climbs are recomputed from every cell that reaches them.

solutions.title: DFS with a memo
solutions.idea: best[r][c] = 1 + the best of the strictly higher neighbours, computed once per cell. Values strictly rise, so there are no cycles and no visited set is needed.

solutions.title: Fill cells from the highest value down
solutions.idea: Sorting cells by value, high to low, is a topological order of the 'step up' arrows. Each cell's higher neighbours are finished before it, so no recursion is needed.

followups: Return the cells of one longest climb, not just its length.
Steps may also go to an equal neighbour, but never twice through the same cell. Why does the memo stop working?
Solve it in O(R · C) without sorting and without recursion. (Hint: count each cell's higher neighbours and peel off local peaks layer by layer.)
